svg.title: Twelve names, twice
svg.desc: A drawn plate of the names on the high priest's stones. Two onyx shoulder stones, his right shoulder on the viewer's left, carry six names each in birth order: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali (25 letters), and Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin (25 letters), following Rashi on Exodus 28:10, with Josephus placing the elder sons on the right. Gold chains run down to the breastpiece, which hangs from the shoulder stones' settings (Exodus 28:25). The breastpiece's twelve stones are shown with the tribe each tradition puts on it: 1, ʾodem: Reuben; 2, pitdah: Simeon; 3, bareqet: Levi; 4, nofekh: Judah; 5, sappir: birth order Dan, Numbers Rabbah Issachar, Exodus Rabbah Issachar; 6, yahalom: birth order Naphtali, Numbers Rabbah Zebulun, Exodus Rabbah Zebulun; 7, leshem: birth order Gad, Numbers Rabbah Dan, Exodus Rabbah Dan; 8, shevo: birth order Asher, Numbers Rabbah Gad, Exodus Rabbah Naphtali; 9, ʾachlamah: birth order Issachar, Numbers Rabbah Naphtali, Exodus Rabbah Gad; 10, tarshish: birth order Zebulun, Numbers Rabbah Asher, Exodus Rabbah Asher; 11, shoham: Joseph; 12, yashpeh: Benjamin. Every tradition agrees on stones 1 to 4 and 11 to 12; Scripture names none. Five echoes between a stone and its tribe are set out, each marked with the order it needs: Dan: The seventh stone’s name is the name of the city Dan took: they “fought against Leshem, captured it … and renamed it after their father Dan” (Joshua 19:47, BSB). The same word appears only there and at Exodus 28:19 and 39:12. Numbers and Exodus Rabbah put Dan on it; birth order puts Gad there. Joseph: Joseph’s stone is the stone of the two shoulder pieces, the ones that carry all twelve names (28:9, 20), and “the birthright belonged to Joseph” (1 Chronicles 5:2, ESV). In the Hebrew only: the Greek has emerald on the shoulders and beryl for the eleventh stone. Levi: bareqet is “the flashing one”, from baraq, lightning. Moses gives the Urim, probably “lights”, to Levi (Deuteronomy 33:8), and Numbers Rabbah paints the Urim and Thummim on Levi’s banner. An echo of sense and nothing more. Benjamin: Of Benjamin: the LORD “dwells between his shoulders” (Deuteronomy 33:12, ESV), and Benjamin’s stone hung between the priest’s. Jerusalem lay in Benjamin’s lot (Joshua 18:28). yashpeh is the word Greek writes iaspis, jasper, the city’s first foundation (Revelation 21:19), though the Septuagint renders it onychion here. Reuben: The first stone is “the red one”, from ʾadom, red. Numbers Rabbah dyes Reuben’s banner red and paints on it the mandrakes he found (Genesis 30:14). A colour, no more. Last, the 22 Hebrew letters, with the 4 the twelve names lack marked in gold; the Talmud says the patriarchs' names and 'the tribes of Jeshurun' were added, which supplies them (Yoma 73b). The plate closes with Exodus 28:12 and 28:29.
svg.text: On his shoulders and on his heart · Exodus 28:9-30
Each shoulder stone carries six names “in the order of their birth” (Exodus 28:10). The breastpiece
carries one name on each stone and does not say which (28:21). Both are “for remembrance before the
gold chains: the breastpiece hangs from the shoulder stones’ settings (28:25)
As the priest faces you, his right shoulder is on your left. Elder sons on the right: Josephus (Antiquities
3.166). Six and six in birth order with Benjamin spelled in full, as at Genesis 35:18: Rashi on 28:10, which
gives 25 and 25 letters; the Talmud records a view that set Judah first on one stone (Sotah 36a). The stone is
onyx in the Hebrew, emerald in the Greek, sardonyx in Josephus. Letters drawn in square script without vowels;
the engravers used the older Hebrew letters.
Birth order: Josephus (Antiquities 3.169), Targum Pseudo-Jonathan and Rashi on 28:17-21. Leah’s six first
(“Rabbah”): Numbers Rabbah 2:7 and Exodus Rabbah 38:8, which swap Naphtali and Gad (“Num. R.”, “Ex. R.”). Every
tradition agrees on stones 1-4 and 11-12. Which end of a row came first is not stated either; a Hebrew reader
Every tradition puts the same tribe here
WHERE A NAME AND A STONE ECHO
only where Leah’s six come first
The seventh stone’s name is the name of the city Dan took: they “fought against Leshem, captured it … and
renamed it after their father Dan” (Joshua 19:47, BSB). The same word appears only there and at Exodus
28:19 and 39:12. Numbers and Exodus Rabbah put Dan on it; birth order puts Gad there.
Joseph’s stone is the stone of the two shoulder pieces, the ones that carry all twelve names (28:9, 20),
and “the birthright belonged to Joseph” (1 Chronicles 5:2, ESV). In the Hebrew only: the Greek has emerald
on the shoulders and beryl for the eleventh stone.
bareqet is “the flashing one”, from baraq, lightning. Moses gives the Urim, probably “lights”, to Levi
(Deuteronomy 33:8), and Numbers Rabbah paints the Urim and Thummim on Levi’s banner. An echo of sense and
Of Benjamin: the LORD “dwells between his shoulders” (Deuteronomy 33:12, ESV), and Benjamin’s stone hung
between the priest’s. Jerusalem lay in Benjamin’s lot (Joshua 18:28). yashpeh is the word Greek writes
iaspis, jasper, the city’s first foundation (Revelation 21:19), though the Septuagint renders it onychion
The first stone is “the red one”, from ʾadom, red. Numbers Rabbah dyes Reuben’s banner red and paints on
it the mandrakes he found (Genesis 30:14). A colour, no more.
No echo turns up for Simeon or Judah, or for the six middle stones beyond the banners Numbers Rabbah colours like
each tribe’s stone. Scripture draws none of these lines; they are noticed, and marked as such.
The twelve names use 18 of the 22 letters; the four in gold are missing. The Talmud says “Abraham, Isaac and
Jacob” and “the tribes of Jeshurun” were engraved there too, so that every letter was present for the Urim
and Thummim to answer through (Yoma 73b). A tradition, and an exact one: those words supply all four.
“Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders for remembrance.”
“So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel … on his heart.”
After the manner of Clarence Larkin · the-way.lewy.au
